# Process–Material–Performance Trade‑off Exploration of Materials Sintering with Machine Learning Models

Padmalatha Kakanuru1 · Prerit Terway2 · Niraj Jha2 · Kishore Pochiraju1

Received: 24 May 2024 / Accepted: 24 October 2024 / Published online: 13 November 2024 © The Author(s) 2024

Abstract Process-induced porosity, defects, and residual stresses lead to mechanical performance degradation in fiber-reinforced composite and other heterogeneous structures. Physical and chemical processes create complex process–material–performance relationships. Predicting porosity and residual stresses in this context requires computationally burdensome forward simulations and obtaining optimal process settings and calibrating properties of new materials requires solving inverse problems with predictions from the forward simulations. In this paper, we parameterized the process–material–performance space and created a dataset based on physics models that are valid for sintering ceramic powders. The dataset was used to train several machine learning models that captured the process–material–performance relationships. The trained ML models were applied in process optimization, calibration of properties for new material systems, and estimating performance for a given process and material. Support vector regression (SVR), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) called REPAIRS were selected, and their prediction accuracy was determined. While the SVR and CNN models require training several models, we show that the GMM model captures the process–material–performance relationships with a single machine-learned model and partial system completion methods. The paper describes root-mean-square error and mean absolute percentage errors of the inferences from the models on a validation dataset.

Keywords  Material calibration · Process design · Performance optimization · Sintering · Machine learning · Multioutput regression · REPAIRS

## Introduction

The thermomechanical performance of structures with heterogeneous materials is the result of complex interactions between the manufacturing process decisions and the resulting micro- and macro-material structures. Process (and mold tools when relevant) parameters such as the temperature and pressure cycles and print orientations in additive manufacturing determine the material microstructures and, thus, the effective properties of the materials. The performance of the structures is directly related to the geometry (design choices, e.g., wall thickness) and the local material properties. These relationships have been explored for fiber-filled composites manufactured with injection molding, transfer molding, or autoclave processes using high-fidelity process–structure–property modeling. Design and process optimization, however, requires solving inverse problems using expensive simulations to evaluate objective and constraint functions in optimization loops. We describe machine learning models that can capture the process–material–performance relationships from a dataset generated with a finite number of samples of the design space. The models are then used to solve performance predictions, calibrate material properties from limited experiments, and optimize process parameters. In this paper, we considered particle sintering, which is a heat treatment process for manufacturing metals and ceramics utilizing powder metallurgy techniques. During sintering, loose or weakly bonded powders in green parts consolidate and become solid parts. In sintering, the temperature is increased to a fixed isothermal temperature, maintained for the required time, and decreased to room temperature with or without adding pressure. During the sintering process, the neck formation between the particles takes place through mass transport mechanisms such

as diffusion, viscous flow, and evaporation at the atomic level, and the ceramic particles will be bonded together at the expense of surface energy. Shaping or forming the green bodies and the sintering processes dictate the microstructure–property performance of final solid parts. The final dimensions, density, and mechanical properties of the required design parts are controlled by heat cycle parameters and densification kinetics of the material. During sintering, 55–64% green body density of many ceramics goes up to 90–100% of their theoretical bulk density [1]. For example, the stereolithography (SLA)- printed preceramic polymers undergo a linear shrinkage of about 30% and volumetric shrinkage of about 65% [2, 3]. The SLA-printed green bodies experience anisotropic shrinkage in sintering due to changes in the morphologies induced by the build orientation [4]. As a result, the shrinkage in the printing direction is higher than in the other directions and varies with the temperature or the resin used in the experiment. In addition, there is always a residual or critical porosity in the printing direction beyond which the densification cannot happen. The shrinkage results in additional post-processing, such as machining and grinding to the size of the required dimensions. Thus, predicting shrinkage and distortion during sintering helps to design the green body geometry to get the desired final dimensions and eliminate additional post-processing. Green bodies are currently designed using empirical scale factors to accommodate this shrinkage. However, this methodology requires a lot of trial-and-error experiments, which are time-consuming and expensive. In this scenario, the accurate sintering process models and simulation techniques help to automate the design of green body shape/ size to produce any final part design. In the literature, various sintering models are available at atomic, microscopic, and macroscopic scales [5–12]. Among these, the macroscopic phenomenological model of Skorohod–Olevsky viscous sintering (SOVS) is widely used for metals [13] and ceramics [14–16] because of its simplicity and accuracy. Machine learning models have been used to surrogate the material behavior during sintering [17, 18]. Numerical simulation of sintering models efficiently predicts the shrinkage, relative density, and associated residual stress states for complex-shaped ceramics. The main challenge with numerical models is that they require many material parameters to predict sintered part dimensions accurately. Finding the material parameters, such as viscosity constants and surface energy, is highly complex due to the expensive experimental measurements and additional analysis required. Usually, optimization techniques are used to calibrate the material parameters required for the simulation of sintering if the heat cycle and relative density and shrinkage of the part are known [16, 19]. However, these techniques are highly time-consuming. Hence,

Machine learning models have recently demonstrated great promise in designing and optimizing additive manufacturing/sintering processes to improve material properties. Jahan et al. The data required for training the model were generated using computational fluid dynamics simulations. Among the K-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), artificial neural network (ANN), and random forest (RF) techniques, de Abreu et al. found that SVM was more promising in predicting the bulk density using the hold time and the electric current density for flash sintered ceramics. The data required for training the models were derived from experiments [21]. A Gaussian process regression machine learning model was developed by Wang et al. [22] to predict the power factor of photonic sintered n-type solid-state thermoelectric films based on four process variables: voltage, pulse duration, the number of pulses, and pulse delay. Kamal T et al. [23] tested the linear regression (LR), K-nearest neighbors (KNN), decision trees (DT), and random forest (RF) machine learning models to predict the relative sintered density of powder metallurgy processed bronze for the given material composition and sintering process parameters. The experimental evaluation demonstrated that the RF model best fits the four models, with a mean absolute error of 1.82%. Suzuki A. et al. [24] explored the laser parameters for suppressing the WC decomposition region in a laser powder bed fusion fabricated WC/Co composite using a convolutional neural network (CNN). Hence, machine learning techniques efficiently explore the sintered parts’ material–process and performance parameters. Minimal literature data on applying machine learning models to design the sintering process are available. Hence, this work explores SVM and Gaussian mixture models to predict the material, process, and performance parameters for pressureless sintering. Here, numerical simulations were conducted to predict the relative density, shrinkage, and stress–strain states for the sintered parts, and this data was used for training the machine learning models. The paper is organized into different sections. The process–material–performance relationships for the sintering process are described using the SOVS model in Sect. 2. Then, the parameters involved in design space are explained under Sect. 3. The details of four different machine learning models used in this work are given in Sect. 4. Then, the numerical simulations conducted for generating the training data, training of the machine learning models on the data, and prediction errors are substantially described in Sect. 5. We conclude the paper stating the findings in Sect. 6.

## Parameterization of the Material–Process– Performance Spaces

Further, it will be more challenging for 3D-printed ceramics because of anisotropic shrinkage. In these situations, machine learning models are more efficient and costeffective. These models can be trained through expert designs. Since the material properties, heat cycle, and performance metrics are interrelated, three separate machine learning surrogate models can be developed using any two feature types to find the third type, as shown in Fig. 2. The design cycle of part produced with thermal, chemical, and mechanical manufacturing process (e.g., sintering) consists of initial design, verification of material–product performance (defects, residual stresses, dimensional stability) through analysis, and optimizing the part design for the given material and manufacturing choices. A good initial design reduces the design cycle time by lowering the analysis-redesign steps. The sintering process design space features are the material constants, heat cycle, and performance metrics. In the conventional design process, the design analysis is conducted using finite element simulations, and for this, the material constants need to be evaluated experimentally. Since sintering is a complex process, finite element analysis becomes computationally expensive and time-consuming, especially in the absence of material constants.

Performance Prediction Model Surrogate

Prior prediction of performance metrics such as shrinkage, relative density, and residual stresses for the sintered parts helps to design the green part accurately. In the conventional design process, the performance is predicted through finite element simulation of physics-based models or by experimentation with trial and error. Conducting trial experiments is the most expensive and time-consuming. Since the material undergoes transient viscoplastic deformation during sintering, the finite element simulations also involve a large computational time. Hence, a trained surrogate machine learning model can be helpful in prior performance prediction with high accuracy. Material Parameter Calibration Problem

The material parameters in the constitutive models of sintering are more complex to evaluate through experimentation, which is time-consuming and expensive, and it will be more challenging for 3D-printed ceramics because of anisotropic shrinkage. The material parameters are crucial to accurately predict performance through finite element simulations for more complex geometries. One way of finding these material parameters for an unknown material is to calibrate the known performance for the given process parameters using finite element modeling and optimization techniques [19]. However, this methodology is computationally expensive and complex. In this scenario, a machine learning-based surrogate model that focuses on predicting sintering material constants based on the given process parameters and performance metrics as inputs is useful. The training data for the model are process parameters and performance metrics as input features and material constants as output features, as given in Table 2.

Optimized Process Design

Sintering is a heat treatment process. The performance of the sintered part is dependent on the heat treatment process

parameters, for example, hold temperature and hold time. In the traditional design, the effect of process parameters on the performance is predicted using experimentation or simulations, which are time-consuming and expensive. Usually, industry standards follow a higher limit of heat cycle temperatures for sintering to achieve higher quality and reliable performance. But sometimes, just the higher temperatures in the cycle may not yield better performance. So, the prior prediction of the optimal heat cycle saves energy and reduces the cost of ceramics manufacturing. As explained earlier, experimental and computational studies involve higher costs for designing and optimizing the sintering heat treatment process; hence, a surrogate model is required. Training a machine learning model on the performance and material space as inputs and the heat cycle parameters as outputs, as given in Table 3, is fast and efficient.

## Machine Learning Models

The design exploration of sintering is a multioutput regression problem with multivariate input feature space and multivariate output space. Machine learning models, such as linear regression (LR), K-nearest neighbors (KNN) regression, decision tree regression, artificial neural networks (ANNs), and random forest regression, support multioutput regression inherently. Zhao et al. have shown that in material behavior modeling, the results of multioutput SVR are comparable to ANNs in accuracy [27]. SVR approaches are more robust and highly recommended for engineering design problems. Hence in this work, SVR models, convolutional neural network (CNN) model, and Gaussian mixture models (REPAIRS) [28] techniques are used to explore the design space of the sintering material–process–performance.

Support Vector Regression Model

Support vector regression is a supervised machine learning model where it returns a continuous-real valued output. The support vector regression (SVR) does not inherently support multioutput regression, and individual SVRs are needed to predict the outputs one at a time as shown in Fig. 3a. Hence, researchers developed different methods for predicting multiple outputs simultaneously at the given input. [29–33]. To solve the multioutput regression problem, one method to apply regression models such as SVR designed for predicting one value for multioutput regression is to divide the multioutput regression problem into multiple sub-problems for each output variable to be predicted. In Scikit-learn, MultiOutputRegressor class supports this approach where it takes the given regressor model as an argument and creates one instance of the given model for each targeted output as shown in Fig. 3b. In this work, the multiple support vector regression models were trained on the dataset to find out the missing performance, process, and material parameter values from design space of 16 parameters. The performance parameters were predicted using the material and process parameters as input features using both single SVR model and multioutput SVR model. For example, a single-output SVR was trained with all the material and process parameters as input features to find out one of the performance parameters, relative density at the end of sintering cycle as output, whereas using the same material and process parameters as input space,

a multioutput SVR model was trained to predict all the 6 performance parameters as output. For single SVR models, six SVRs were trained, one for each of the performance parameters as outputs (10 inputs x 1 output) and two for process design (15 inputs x 1 output). For calibrating the material parameters, the values of the other known material parameters were used as inputs along with performance and process parameters as inputs and predicted only one missing parameter (15 inputs x 1 output), while for multioutput SVR models, one SVR was trained for 6 performance parameters as output (10 inputs x 6 outputs), another SVR was trained for 2 process parameters (14 inputs x 2 outputs) and another SVR was trained for 8 material parameters as output (8 inputs x 8 outputs). Convolutional Neural Network Model

We trained several convolutional neural network models from the dataset to infer missing performance, process, and material parameter values from the 16-parameter design space. The performance parameters were predicted individually, with the material and process parameters as the input features. For example, a CNN was trained with all the material and process parameters as input features. One of the performance parameters is the relative density at the end of the sintering cycle ( 휌f ) as the output. The neural network model thus trained can infer the final relative density of the sintered part for a given material selection and process design. This neural network model serves as a surrogate for the SOVS model and obtains the final density result without the need for the finite element analysis of the entire sintering cycle using a physics-based model. Six such CNNs were trained, one for each of the performance parameters as outputs (10 inputs x 1 output), two for process design (14 inputs x 1 output), and eight for calibrating material parameters (15 inputs x 1 output). When calibrating the material parameters, we used the values of the other known parameters as inputs and inferred only one missing parameter. The architecture used is shown in Table 5. The batch size and the number of training epochs were set at 100. Each neural network is trained in roughly 20-30 s on an NVidia RTX A6000 GPU. The performance of the CNN models in terms of the RMS errors and MAPE is described in Sect. 5.2.

If the pdf value is above a threshold (1 in our case), we accept the predicted value of the missing parameter. However, a low pdf value indicates a low confidence in our prediction. In this case, we sweep over several (20,000 and 100,000 in our case) possible values of the missing parameters within its specified range. We also concatenate the possible values of the missing parameters with the values in the training set (in case any of those are a good estimate of the missing parameters). Next, we determine the pdf value of the possible system completions with each of these possibilities of the missing values. Sweeping over multiple possible values of the missing features also helps capture multimodal system behavior. Multimodal behavior arises when several possible combinations of the missing values are good estimates of those missing features. If we determine a combination with a high pdf value, we use that as a possible completion of the missing values. In case a user desires multiple possible completions to capture the multimodal response, they can use several completions with a pdf value above a threshold. If, after sweeping, we still do not obtain a system completion with a high pdf value, REPAIRS fails to determine the missing parameters. In this paper, we used REPAIRS for three different scenarios. ## Exploration of Process–Material– Performance Space for Sintering

In this work, single-output SVR and multioutput support vector regression algorithm available in Python Scikit-learn, known as direct (MultiOutputRegressor), CNN, and REPAIRS technique, were used to explore the sintering material–process–performance design space. The predictions were arrived in three steps. Material and heat treatment process parameters were considered as input features, and performance metrics were used as output labels in the first step. In the second step, the heat cycle and performance parameters were considered as input features and the material parameters as output labels.

In the third step, the material and performance parameters were considered as input features and heat cycle parameters as output labels.

Training Dataset Generation

For the exploration of sintering design space, 10,000 data points were generated using Latin Hypercube sampling with the range of values as given in Table 6 for material and heat cycle parameters (8 materials and 2 processes). The sintering heat cycle process considered here consists of heating the green bodies from 300◦C to the sintering hold temperature ( Th ) at the rate of 3 ◦C/min, holding ( th ) at the sintering hold temperature, and cooling the sintered parts to the room temperature at a rate of 10◦C/min as shown in Fig. 5. The finite element simulations were conducted for the single-element axisymmetric model with a radius of 5 mm and height of 5 mm, as shown in Fig. 6, to predict the performance parameters for the dataset of 10,000 points. The SOVS model as explained in Sect. 2 was implemented for the axisymmetric model using a user-defined creep subroutine and visco-analysis in commercial finite element software Simulia [37]. The incremental viscoplastic strain in the creep subroutine of Simulia software is computed as the sum of incremental swelling or shrinkage strain and the incremental creep strain as follows.

Validation of Machine Learning Models

The validation of performance predictions was carried out using multioutput SVR for two case studies. Here are the details of the two case studies.

Case Study 1

In this case study, the sintering design space of 3D-printed alumina (Al2O3 ) ceramic cylindrical parts taken from the reference [16] is explored. The material and the sintering process parameters given in Table 10 were used for the predicting the performance parameters using multioutput SVR. While the sintering cycle used as per the reference work did not have hold time at sintering temperature which is the required parameter for the model, 2 sec was considered at the sintering temperature of 1700◦C for the predictions. In addition, among the Qv and 휂0 values given in the reference work the values that were representative of Arrhenius viscosity law [26] are chosen for predictions. The performance surrogate model was able to accurately predict the final relative density 휌f as 0.89. However, the other performance metrics such as residual stress and strain values were not given in the reference work to compare with the model predictions.

## Concluding Remarks

Sintering is a thermo-viscoplastic process, and simulating it requires valid and multiple material behavior models. Such numerical simulations require substantial computational time to predict a given material and process plan’s performance outcomes (density, shrinkages, and residual stresses). Often, solutions to the inverse problems, i.e., finding calibrated material parameters for a given process and performance parameter set, are desired or finding the optimized process plan for a new material to yield desired performance outcomes. Solving the inverse problems requires many forward simulations

We defined three scenarios: computationally efficient surrogate for the performance prediction problem, inverse problem solution for material property calibration, and process parameter

optimization. The three problems are solved using four specific machine learning models. The models used were single-output SVR, multioutput SVR, CNN, and Gaussian mixture model (GMM), referred to as REPAIRS.
